bird-of-paradise.webp: A bird of paradise, its long tail feathers curling, perches on a flowering branch drawn in fine lines of gold on a black ground. Janoszanka built her pictures from countless small, exact strokes, more like a jeweller or a lacquer-maker than a painter, and she signed this one in the lower left corner.
butterfly.webp: A great butterfly, patterned in blue and gold, hovers over still water beside an old tree whose bark is drawn as rings of gold line. Threads of silver fall from the branches like rain or cobweb. As in all her pictures, Janoszanka sets bright, jewel-like colour against a dark ground.
spring.webp: Janoszanka’s spring is a pond in a strange wood: white water lilies open on the dark water, striped trunks rise like columns, and long streamers of green and violet hang from the branches like new growth. In the corner a fat, spotted toad sits watching. Like her Winter, it turns a season into a fairy tale.
winter.webp: Two black birds, crows or ravens, face each other in a snowbound wood, one with its beak open as if calling to the other. Stars of frost fill the air, icicles hang from the branches and the trunks are traced in gold. Janoszanka makes winter not bleak but glittering.
cassatt-francoise-holding-a-little-dog-l: Françoise, a young girl, sat for a whole series of Cassatt’s pastels around 1909, in different dresses and hats and poses; the long titles, like this one, tell them apart. Here she holds a small black dog in her lap and looks away past us. Pastel let Cassatt draw and colour at once: the quick strokes of the dress set off the smoothly worked face. The picture is in the High Museum of Art in Atlanta.
gogh-the-poets-garden.webp: This is the little public garden across from the Yellow House, Van Gogh’s home in Arles. In the autumn of 1888 he painted it several times as The Poet’s Garden, to hang in the room he had ready for Paul Gauguin, and imagined the old Italian poets Petrarch and Boccaccio walking there. The picture is now in the Art Institute of Chicago.
renoir-child-with-brown-hair.webp: This little head is hardly bigger than a playing card, under 12 centimetres high. Renoir painted many such small studies of children, catching a face in a few soft touches and leaving the canvas bare around it. It is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
renoir-child-with-blond-hair.webp: Smaller still than its brown-haired companion, this sketch measures under 10 centimetres, and Renoir signed it with a single R. In the late 1890s he painted his own children again and again, among them his son Jean with his long fair hair; whose face this is, nobody can say for sure.
renoir-woman-arranging-her-hat.webp: A young woman in a pink dress sits in the grass and raises both hands to settle her straw hat. Around 1890 Renoir often painted young women out of doors like this, the leaves and grass laid in as feathery dabs of colour while the figure is softly rounded. The painting is in the High Museum of Art in Atlanta.
renoir-nude-in-a-chair.webp: A bather sits on a red armchair, bending to her foot with a white cloth across her lap. In the mid-1880s, after seeing Raphael’s work in Italy, Renoir drew his figures with firmer outlines than before, and pastel suited that clear drawing. The picture is in the High Museum of Art in Atlanta.
toulouse-lautrec-a-woman-and-a-man-on-ho: Lautrec drew this when he was about sixteen. Two falls in his early teens had broken both his legs, which never grew properly again, and he could no longer ride, but he drew horses constantly, as here, in quick lines of graphite and blue crayon. The small sheet is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
toulouse-lautrec-the-clown-m-joret.webp: A clown with a towering hat and a great black moustache, set down in a few dashing strokes of the pen. The red monogram in the lower corner is the stamp put on the works found in Lautrec’s studio after his death. The drawing is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
toulouse-lautrec-albert-grenier.webp: Albert Grenier was a fellow student of Lautrec’s in the Paris studio of the painter Fernand Cormon, and a close friend; for a time Lautrec lodged with him and his wife Lili in Montmartre. The portrait is painted on a small wooden panel, and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
toulouse-lautrec-woman-in-the-garden-of-: Monsieur Forest kept a large garden near Lautrec’s studio in Montmartre, and there Lautrec painted his models in the open air. The paint is thin and quick, with the canvas showing between the strokes, so the picture keeps the freshness of a sketch. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
toulouse-lautrec-the-streetwalker.webp: A woman in a pointed yellow hat stands on a garden path among trees, looking straight out at us. Lautrec often painted on plain cardboard, as here, letting its warm brown show through thin, quick strokes of colour. The picture is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
toulouse-lautrec-the-sofa.webp: Two women lounge on a sofa, at ease and unaware of the painter. In the mid-1890s Lautrec spent days at a time in the Paris brothels, painting the women there in their idle hours, plainly and without judging them. This is one of those pictures, painted on cardboard; it is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
toulouse-lautrec-woman-before-a-mirror.w: A woman stands with her back to us before a tall mirror, a red curtain beside her. Lautrec painted it in 1897 on cardboard, in quick, loose strokes, and shows her as she is, with no attempt to flatter. The picture is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
toulouse-lautrec-emilie.webp: A woman in a yellow jacket and a black-plumed hat stands in a sunny park while a rider goes by behind her. Lautrec left much of the wooden panel barely painted, setting down only what he needed. The picture is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
toulouse-lautrec-mademoiselle-nys.webp: Lautrec painted this quick portrait on a bare wooden panel in 1899 and wrote across its top corner a dedication to the Nys family, with his name and the year. That year he spent some months in a clinic at Neuilly, outside Paris, after a breakdown. The panel is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
toulouse-lautrec-at-the-circus-the-spani: In 1899 Lautrec was shut away in a clinic at Neuilly after a breakdown. To show the doctors that his mind and memory were sound, he drew a series of circus scenes from memory, about forty of them, of which this is one. A rider in a top hat puts his horse through the Spanish walk, a show step in which the horse lifts its forelegs high, while two clowns watch from the ring.
toulouse-lautrec-two-dogs.webp: A long-nosed dog with a curling tail and, beside it, the head of a small one, each set down in a few wiry lines of pen and brown ink. The strip of paper is only 7.5 centimetres high. Lautrec loved dogs and drew them all his life; this sheet is undated and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
corot-landscape.webp: Feathery trees, a still river, a boat by the bank and a far-off house under a pale sky. In his last years Corot painted many such quiet scenes in the studio, from memory rather than on the spot, in soft silvery greys and greens; they were the pictures that made him famous. This one is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
durand-in-the-woods.webp: Tall trees close overhead like the arches of a church, while light breaks into a clearing far down the path. Asher Durand led the Hudson River School after Thomas Cole’s death, and in 1855, the year of this picture, he published his Letters on Landscape Painting, urging painters to study nature closely, tree by tree. The painting is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
kensett-eatons-neck-long-island.webp: A pale beach curves away under a wide, empty sky above calm water: almost nothing, painted with great care. Kensett made it in the summer of 1872, the last of his life. The pictures found in his studio after his death that December, known as his Last Summer’s Work, were given to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where this one hangs.
heade-newburyport-meadows.webp: Haystacks stand in the salt marshes near Newburyport, Massachusetts, while a storm passes and the sun breaks through. Heade painted more than a hundred pictures of such marshes, watching how the light and weather changed over the flat land. This one is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
klimt-mada-primavesi.webp: Mäda Primavesi was nine when Klimt painted her, standing squarely with her feet apart, sure of herself, in a white dress against a ground of flowers and violet. Her father, Otto Primavesi, a banker, was one of Klimt’s patrons. Mäda lived until 2000, and the painting is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
klimt-standing-nude.webp: Klimt drew constantly, often from models who walked about his studio, and left thousands of drawings like this one, in a light, searching graphite line. The stamp in the corner, ‘Gustav Klimt Nachlass’, marks a sheet from his estate. The drawing is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
klimt-reclining-nude.webp: A woman lies stretched out, her head thrown back, drawn in a few long, unbroken pencil lines. In the years around 1912 Klimt made hundreds of such drawings of reclining women, and the line itself, flowing and supple, matters as much as the figure. The sheet is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
klimt-reclining-nude-with-drapery.webp: A woman curls on her side, half wrapped in a patterned cloth whose spots and swirls Klimt marks in pencil, much as he filled his paintings with ornament. Drawings like this were made for their own sake, not as studies for paintings. The sheet is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Klimt drew the same model twice on one sheet, once from close above and once lower down, trying the pose from different sides. The pencil runs quickly over the folds of her dress. The drawing is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
klimt-reclining-nude-with-drapery-back-v: A woman lies with her back to us, her hair and a loose drapery spreading around her in long, rippling lines. It is one of Klimt’s last drawings: he died in February 1918, after a stroke. The sheet is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
klimt-half-figure-of-a-young-woman.webp: A young woman with braided hair and closed eyes, drawn in pencil in 1918, in the last weeks of Klimt’s life. The sheet carries his estate’s stamp, and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
crane-woman-seated-on-a-sofa.webp: A woman in a dark green dress and yellow shawl sits on a blue sofa, a book in her hand, with blue-and-white china on the cabinet behind. Such china was the height of artistic fashion in the 1870s, part of the Aesthetic Movement Crane belonged to. The tiny watercolour, under 18 centimetres wide, is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
crane-italian-farmhouse.webp: Crane married in 1871 and spent the next two years in Italy, much of the time in Rome, painting watercolours like this one of an old farmhouse half hidden by trees. The picture is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
crane-valentine.webp: In the 1870s Crane designed valentine cards, printed in many colours and gold and set in lace paper, as this one is. A young man in pink and a young woman in green meet at a stile among flowers, dressed in the fashions of about 1800, which Crane loved to draw. The card is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
crane-valentine-765291.webp: A young woman in a long pink gown reaches up to pick blossom from a tree, with lilies growing behind her. Crane designed it as a valentine card, printed in colours and gold, in 1876. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
crane-valentine-767102.webp: A young man in a patchwork tunic blows a horn beneath a window, where a young woman in blue leans out to listen; the words To My Love run along the foot. Crane designed it as a valentine card, printed in colours and gold, in 1876. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
crane-design-for-trade-card.webp: A warrior drives a chariot behind galloping horses, with empty banners above and below left for the words. Crane drew it in pen and brown ink as a design for a trade card, a small advertising card, for the Sun Life Assurance Society. The drawing is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
crane-dancing-nymph.webp: A nymph dances with a tambourine against a dark tangle of vines, her dress swirling around her. Crane made the lithograph in 1895 for L’Estampe originale, a Paris series of original prints by artists from many countries. The print is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
leonardo-da-vinci-head-of-a-man-in-profi: A man with heavy features and a mop of curls, drawn in pen over black chalk on a scrap of paper less than 12 centimetres high. Leonardo drew many such profiles in his years in Milan. He was left-handed, and his shading runs from upper left to lower right, the natural stroke for that hand. The sheet is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
michelangelo-two-nudes-fighting.webp: Two men wrestle, drawn in quick, strong pen strokes on a scrap of paper only 8 centimetres high. Michelangelo drew it around 1505, the years when he was planning a great painting of soldiers, the Battle of Cascina, for the city hall of Florence, which was never finished. The sheet is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
stella-coney-island.webp: In 1913 Stella went to the Mardi Gras at Coney Island, New York’s great seaside amusement park, and was dazzled by its electric lights, crowds and rides. In this round picture he breaks them into shards of colour, in the manner of the Italian Futurists, who wanted to paint speed, noise and light. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
stella-dog-in-motion.webp: A dog races by, its head stretched forward and its fur streaming. Like the Italian Futurists, Stella wanted to paint movement itself, not a still moment. The picture is in the Harvard Art Museums.
stella-skyscrapers.webp: The towers of New York rise in grey and blue washes of watercolour, a window frame cutting across them. Around 1920 Stella was working on his great series The Voice of the City of New York, and the skyscrapers were a subject he came back to again and again. This sheet is in the Buffalo AKG Art Museum.
stella-tree-of-my-life.webp: A great tree rises through a dense garden of flowers, birds and leaves. Painted in 1919, it marks Stella’s turn from the machines and lights of the city towards nature, and as its title says, it stands for his own life. It is in a private collection.
stella-tropical-sonata.webp: A dark palm spreads its spiky leaves against a fiery sky. Stella gave several of his pictures musical names, as here; in the 1920s he painted more and more of tropical plants and flowers. The picture is in the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York.
stella-sirens.webp: In Greek myth the Sirens sang so sweetly that sailors steered onto the rocks to hear them. Stella paints them as smooth, glowing figures among tropical flowers and shells, in the bright, polished style of his later years. The picture is in a private collection.
stella-self-portrait.webp: Stella painted himself as a young man, a few years after arriving in New York from Italy, in the dark, rich style he learned from his teacher William Merritt Chase. Beside him stands a pot shaped like a cabbage. It is a long way from the bright colours he would paint later.
decamp-the-blue-mandarin-coat.webp: A red-haired woman stands with her hands on her hips in a Chinese robe, its sleeves lined with orange and edged with embroidery. Robes like this were a favourite prop of the Boston painters. DeCamp painted it in 1922, the year before he died, and it is in the High Museum of Art in Atlanta.
decamp-the-listener.webp: A young woman leans forward, all attention, her shoulders bare above a dress of black lace. We seem to look down at her from just above, as from the next seat at the theatre. It is in a private collection.
decamp-carnation-and-black.webp: A young woman in an orange-red dress, black lace and a broad black hat sits in profile before an orange curtain. The title names the colours rather than the sitter, as Whistler did with his paintings. The picture is in the Currier Museum of Art in Manchester, New Hampshire.
decamp-sally.webp: A girl in a white sailor blouse with a black neckerchief looks thoughtfully aside. DeCamp was known for his careful drawing and the cool light on his figures. The painting is in the Worcester Art Museum, Massachusetts.
decamp-portrait-of-edith-the-artists-wif: An oval portrait of Edith, the painter’s wife, in a dark dress against a warm brown ground. Her steady gaze and slight smile make it one of DeCamp’s most direct portraits. It is in a private collection.
decamp-our-nanny.webp: The DeCamp family’s nanny, in a high-collared black dress with a small brooch, smiles quietly to herself. A portrait painted for the family rather than for show. It is in a private collection.
decamp-portrait-of-a-young-lady.webp: A young woman in a soft white gown, holding a pink flower, sits against a blue ground painted in loose, sweeping strokes. The face is carefully finished while the dress and background are freely brushed. It is in a private collection.
decamp-gloucester.webp: Fishing schooners lie in the harbour of Gloucester, Massachusetts, seen from a wharf, their masts reflected in the grey water. Gloucester was a busy fishing port and a favourite summer place for painters. The picture is in the Cincinnati Art Museum, in the city where DeCamp was born.
decamp-red-roofs.webp: Red-roofed houses peep between tall, slender trees on a sunny hillside, painted in the broken strokes of the Impressionists. It is undated, and in a private collection.
decamp-street-scene-in-venice.webp: A quiet street in Venice, with tall houses, a stone well-head and a strip of blue sky. DeCamp was one of the young Americans who followed their teacher Frank Duveneck to Italy around 1880, and he painted this there in 1881. It is in the Cincinnati Art Museum.
rossetti-the-loving-cup.webp: A woman in red raises a golden cup, as if offering a toast, against a wall of brass dishes. A loving cup is a cup shared among friends or lovers, each drinking in turn. Rossetti painted many such half-length women in the 1860s, rich in colour and pattern. The picture is in the National Museum of Western Art in Tokyo.
hunt-the-lantern-makers-courtship.webp: On a street in Cairo, a young lantern maker reaches out to touch the face of a girl beneath her veil, trying to learn what she looks like. Hunt began the picture in Cairo in 1854, on his first journey to Egypt and the Holy Land. It is in the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery.
brown-the-irish-girl.webp: A girl with a great mass of dark, curling hair, wrapped in a red shawl, holds a blue cornflower and looks sideways out of the picture. Brown painted her in 1860 with the close attention of the Pre-Raphaelites. The picture is in the Yale Center for British Art.
brown-carrying-corn.webp: Low evening sun lights the stooks and the hay carts on a field at harvest time. Brown painted this small picture out of doors near his home at Finchley, north of London. It is in Tate Britain.
hughes-self-portrait.webp: Arthur Hughes painted himself at nineteen, and wrote his age on the canvas. Shortly before, reading The Germ, the Pre-Raphaelites’ own magazine, had won him over to their ideas. The portrait is in the National Portrait Gallery in London.
hughes-a-christmas-carol-at-bracken-dene: A family of children gathers round as one of the girls plays the violin. It is a group portrait painted in 1878–1879, the children in matching blue and black, and full of character. The picture is in the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery.
hughes-home-from-sea.webp: A young sailor, back from sea, lies face down on his mother’s grave, while his sister in mourning sits beside him. Hughes painted the churchyard at Chingford, in Essex, outdoors and in close detail, and added the sister some years after he began. The picture is in the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford.
hughes-mrs-leathart-and-her-three-childr: Mrs Leathart sits with her three children on a balcony under an arch, with doves at their feet. Her husband, James Leathart, a manufacturer in Newcastle, was one of the great collectors of Pre-Raphaelite painting. The picture is in the Laing Art Gallery in Newcastle.
hughes-the-potters-courtship.webp: On a rocky shore above the sea, a young potter shows his clay figure to a girl who sits spinning. The story is told by the little red statuette between them. The picture is in the Laing Art Gallery in Newcastle.
hughes-uncertainty.webp: A young woman in a long dress pauses in a doorway, a tall hound beside her, her hand on the rail. Her face and the title leave us to guess what she is unsure of. It is in a private collection.
hughes-silver-and-gold.webp: Two women walk together in a garden, one young in a rich red gown, the other old, in black with a white ruff, as if to set youth beside age. A peacock rests beside them. It is in a private collection.
hughes-the-landslip.webp: A cliff where the land has slid away into a turquoise sea, with gorse and heather in bloom in front. Hughes painted landscapes more and more in his last years; he died in December 1915. The picture is in a private collection.
burne-jones-the-wizard.webp: In a room crowded with strange instruments, a hooded wizard draws back a curtain to show a young woman a vision in a round magic mirror. Burne-Jones worked on the picture through much of the 1890s. It is in the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery.
stillman-a-lady-with-peacocks-in-a-garde: A young woman walks down the steps of a terraced garden while peacocks trail their tails over the walls, with cypresses and Italian hills beyond. Stillman lived in Italy for many years, in Rome and Florence, and painted its gardens often. It is in a private collection.
stillman-afternoon-in-the-colonna-garden: The garden of the Palazzo Colonna in Rome climbs the hill behind the palace in steep terraces. Stillman, who lived in Rome while her husband was a newspaper correspondent there, peoples it with women, a child, flowers and a peacock. It is in a private collection.
de-morgan-the-angel-of-death.webp: A great dark angel, a scythe in his hand, bends over a young woman, who reaches up to him not in fear but in welcome. De Morgan saw death not as an end but as a passing into a higher life. She painted this in 1880, at twenty-five, and it is in the De Morgan Collection.
de-morgan-earthbound.webp: A rich old man in a golden robe crouches over his gold, while an angel above him spreads her wings and a figure of light waits far off in the sky. He will not look up: he is earthbound, held down by his wealth. The picture is in the De Morgan Collection.
de-morgan-moonbeams-dipping-into-the-sea: De Morgan turns moonbeams into three young women who slide down from the moon one after another, hand in hand, until the last touches the sea. Her pictures often give shapes to light, the elements and the soul. It is in the De Morgan Collection.
de-morgan-the-sea-maidens.webp: Five sea maidens hold hands in the waves, waist-deep among the rocks of a quiet coast. The pale figures standing in a row echo the art of the early Italian Renaissance that De Morgan loved. The picture is in the De Morgan Collection.
waterhouse-destiny.webp: A young woman drinks from a blue bowl before a round window, through which ships set out to sea. Waterhouse painted it in 1900, for an exhibition raising money for the families of soldiers fighting in the Boer War, and she seems to drink to the ships and those who sail in them. It is in Towneley Hall, Burnley.
A woman in a blue cloak sits on the roots of an old tree at dusk, playing a pipe, while the last light burns in the clouds over the dark wood. Hughes worked mostly in watercolour and gouache, building up deep, glowing colour. It is in a private collection.
edward-robert-hughes-a-rainy-sunday.webp: A woman and a girl in bonnets, the woman holding a prayer book, step out on a wet cobbled street while a man shakes his umbrella in a doorway. They wear the fashions of about 1800. Hughes painted it at about twenty-one. It is in a private collection.
edward-robert-hughes-the-princess-out-of: A young princess in a long velvet cloak has escaped her lessons and lies in the grass among the flowers, her hair spread down her back. The picture is in the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne.
edward-robert-hughes-bell-and-dorothy-fr: A portrait of two sisters, one with a violin and the other seated in white with an orange sash, in a room with a window of round glass panes. Hughes was much in demand for portraits of children. It is in a private collection.
leighton-greek-girls-playing-at-ball.web: Two girls throw a ball on a terrace high above the sea, their thin draperies whirling about them in the wind. Leighton often modelled his figures in clay first, to work out a pose before he painted it. The picture is in the Dick Institute in Kilmarnock, Scotland.
leighton-wedded.webp: In an arched doorway above the sea, a husband kisses his wife’s hand as she leans against him. The picture was hugely popular in Leighton’s day and was sold as a print in great numbers. It is in the Art Gallery of New South Wales in Sydney.
leighton-light-of-the-harem.webp: A young woman in a long cream robe stretches her arms above her head while a girl holds up a mirror for her. Leighton travelled in the Middle East and brought back tiles and ideas for his house in London. It is in a private collection.
leighton-portrait-of-may-sartoris.webp: May Sartoris, about fifteen, walks through an autumn landscape in a black riding habit and a broad black hat with a red scarf. Her mother, the singer Adelaide Kemble, was one of Leighton’s closest friends. The portrait is in the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth, Texas.
leighton-may-sartoris-mrs-henry-evans-go: The same May Sartoris whom Leighton painted as a girl, now grown and married, in a pink dress and a veil of white lace. He knew her all her life. The portrait is in Leighton House, his own home in London.
leighton-mrs-james-guthrie.webp: Mrs Guthrie, tall in a black silk dress, arranges lilies in a vase in a richly furnished room. Leighton painted few full-length portraits; this is one of his grandest. It is in the Yale Center for British Art.
leighton-lucia.webp: A young woman’s head in profile, her dark hair caught up, against a dark ground. Leighton painted many such heads, giving them Italian names. This one is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
egypt-mummy-mask-of-a-woman.webp: This mask covered the head and chest of a woman’s mummy in the time when Egypt was ruled by Rome. It is made of cartonnage, layers of linen glued with plaster and painted. The old Egyptian form mixes with Roman fashion: her curly hairstyle, her jewellery and the wreath of flowers on her head. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
egypt-coffin-of-henettawy.webp: Henettawy was a chantress of Amun-Re, a singer in the temple of the god at Thebes. Her coffin, made of wood covered with gesso and painted, is filled with images of gods and protective spells, and was varnished to the yellow colour typical of coffins of her time. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
egypt-funeral-ritual-in-a-garden.webp: A garden with rows of trees and a pool where a boat carries the dead man’s image, while servants bring offerings. This is not the ancient wall itself but a full-size copy, painted in 1921 by the Met’s Egyptian Expedition in the tomb of Nakhtmin at Thebes, to record it. The copy is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
egypt-artists-painting-of-a-hippopotamus: Egyptian artists used flat flakes of limestone as sketchpads, to practise or to try out a figure. On this one, from the reign of Queen Hatshepsut, someone painted a hippopotamus in a few sure strokes of black and red. It is only 12 centimetres wide, and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
egypt-painted-shroud-fragment.webp: A woman’s head in profile, with a heavy black wig and a beaded collar, painted on linen that once wrapped a mummy. Only this piece survives. It dates from the last centuries before Christ or the first after, and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
near-east-jar-with-mountain-goats.webp: A mountain goat with huge sweeping horns stands in a frame of painted bands on this jar from Iran, made about six thousand years ago, before writing was invented. Goats like these were among the favourite subjects of the potters of the region. The jar is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
greece-grave-stele-of-a-little-girl.webp: A little girl holds two doves, bringing one up to kiss it. The stone marked her grave in the time when the Parthenon was being built, and it is carved in fine marble from the island of Paros. It is one of the best-loved Greek works in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
greece-funerary-plaque.webp: A dead man lies on a bier while mourners raise their hands to their heads in grief; below, chariots race, perhaps at his funeral games. Plaques like this, painted in black on red clay, were set into the walls of tombs near Athens. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
anglo-saxon-pendant-with-a-cross.webp: A gold pendant less than 3 centimetres across, with garnets set in the shape of a cross. It was made in the early 600s, when the English were first becoming Christian. Such pendants were worn by women on necklaces. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
anglo-saxon-pendant-with-a-garnet.webp: A gold pendant decorated with spirals of fine gold wire, called filigree, around a large garnet. Behind the garnet lies a thin gold foil stamped with a tiny grid, which makes the stone sparkle. It was made in the early 600s and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
anglo-saxon-bird-brooch.webp: A tiny brooch, about 3 centimetres long, in the shape of a bird of prey with a hooked beak and a garnet eye. Its pin is lost. It was made in the first half of the 500s, when the Anglo-Saxons had only recently settled in England. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
anglo-saxon-sword-pommel.webp: The pommel is the knob at the end of a sword’s hilt. This one is decorated with silver and niello, a black metal paste, in the style of the late 800s, the time of King Alfred. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
anglo-saxon-bird-brooch-with-garnets.web: A tiny brooch shaped like a bird of prey, with a garnet eye and a garnet in its tail, its body worked in gilded silver with black niello lines. Brooches like this were often made in pairs. It dates from the first half of the 500s and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
anglo-saxon-disk-brooch-with-glass.webp: A round brooch, 3 centimetres across, with gold filigree spirals around a centre of red glass, set on silvered bronze. It was made in the 600s and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
anglo-saxon-square-headed-brooch.webp: Square-headed brooches, named for their shape, fastened women’s clothing at the shoulder. This one, of gilded silver, is decorated with deeply cut patterns that catch the light. It was made in the early 500s and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
anglo-saxon-miniature-brooch-with-a-garn: A small square-headed brooch of gilded silver, with a garnet set in its head. It was made in the early 500s and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
anglo-saxon-miniature-square-headed-broo: A small square-headed brooch of gilded silver, its patterns picked out with niello, a black metal paste. It was made in the early 500s and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
saxon-monk-scribe-on-a-wyvern.webp: A monk sits astride a wyvern, a two-legged dragon, writing on a board. It was cast in brass in the mid-1100s, probably in Magdeburg, one of the great centres of metalwork in Saxony. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
saxon-falconer-aquamanile.webp: An aquamanile is a jug for pouring water over the hands, used at table or by a priest at the altar. This one takes the shape of a falconer on horseback; it was filled through an opening in the top and poured through a spout. It was cast in north Germany in the 1200s and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
saxon-rooster-aquamanile.webp: A jug for pouring water over the hands, cast in the shape of a proud rooster, a loop from its back to its head for a handle. Such vessels were made in north Germany in the 1200s. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
saxon-pricket-candlestick.webp: A candle was pressed down onto the spike at the top, called a pricket. The candlestick is decorated with birds and vines in champlevé enamel, made by filling hollows cut in the metal with powdered glass and firing it. It dates from the late 1100s and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
paton-puck-and-fairies.webp: Puck, the mischievous spirit from Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, sits among a crowd of fairies in the dark of the wood. Paton became famous for his fairy paintings from the play. This one is in the Yale Center for British Art.
paton-study-from-nature-inveruglas.webp: Mossy rocks, a stream and old twisted trees at Inveruglas, on the shore of Loch Lomond in Scotland, painted with every leaf and stone in view, as the critic John Ruskin urged artists to do. Paton painted it in 1857. It is in the Yale Center for British Art.
paton-christian-at-the-foot-of-the-cross: In John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress, Christian’s heavy burden falls from his back when he reaches the cross, and three Shining Ones come to greet him. Paton paints that moment, the angels surrounded by light. The picture is in the Aberdeen Art Gallery.
sandys-vivien.webp: Vivien is the enchantress of the Arthurian legends who wins the secrets of the wizard Merlin and traps him with his own spell. Sandys paints her against peacock feathers, with an apple and a sprig of flowers. The picture is in the Manchester Art Gallery.
sandys-grace-rose.webp: A young woman arranges roses in a green bowl. Her name and the year are written at the top of the picture, with her family’s coat of arms, and the roses are a play on her name. The portrait is in the Yale Center for British Art.
sandys-susanna-rose.webp: An old woman in a lace cap and blue ribbons looks steadily out at us, painted with every wrinkle and thread. She was probably of the same family as Grace Rose, whom Sandys painted four years later; their coat of arms appears in the corner. The portrait is in the Cleveland Museum of Art.
sandys-whitlingham-norfolk.webp: Sunset over the river at Whitlingham, just outside Norwich, the city where Sandys was born. The sky glows orange behind a dark line of trees. It is in the Yale Center for British Art.
brett-the-stonebreaker.webp: A boy breaks stones for mending the roads, with a puppy at his side, on a bright summer day. Behind him rises Box Hill in Surrey, painted with such exactness that the trees on its slopes can be counted. The picture is in the Walker Art Gallery in Liverpool.
brett-february-in-the-isle-of-wight.webp: Bare trees on a slope above the sea, on the Isle of Wight in late winter, with a woman walking on the path below. Brett painted with the patient detail of the Pre-Raphaelites. The picture is in the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery.
brett-near-sorrento.webp: The cliffs of Sorrento drop straight into the Bay of Naples, with fishing boats moored below. Brett painted it in 1863. It is in the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery.
brett-southern-coast-of-guernsey.webp: Rocks and islets stretch out from the southern coast of Guernsey, one of the Channel Islands, under a sky of soft pink clouds. Brett, who was also an astronomer, spent his summers sailing round the coasts of Britain with his family, painting as he went. The picture is in the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery.
brett-pwll-cwn.webp: Green cliffs fold down to a quiet bay on the coast of Wales. Brett painted many such coastal views from his summer voyages. It is in the Yale Center for British Art.
brett-man-of-war-rocks-coast-of-dorset.w: Man of War Rocks lie off a small bay near Lulworth on the coast of Dorset, beside the great chalk cliffs. A figure and a rowing boat on the beach show the scale of the cliffs. The picture is in the Yale Center for British Art.
brett-the-shallows-of-hareslade-cove-gow: Tall rocks rise from the still shallows of Hareslade Cove, on the Gower peninsula in south Wales. Brett painted it in 1887. It is in the Yale Center for British Art.
brett-a-view-of-felixstowe.webp: Wooden breakwaters run down into the sea at Felixstowe, on the coast of Suffolk, while steamers and sailing boats pass under a heavy sky. Brett painted it in 1893. It is in the National Gallery of Ireland in Dublin.
anderson-the-song-of-the-lark.webp: A girl lies in the grass, her chin on her hand, gazing up into the sky where a lark is singing out of sight. Anderson painted many such pictures of children, sweet and finely finished. It is in a private collection.
anderson-little-helper.webp: A small girl in a yellow dress sweeps the doorstep with a broom much too big for her, while a kitten plays at her feet. Anderson painted it in 1872. It is in a private collection.
anderson-girl-with-lilac.webp: A girl with long red-brown hair breathes in the scent of a spray of lilac. Anderson often painted children close up like this, filling the picture with a face and flowers. It is in a private collection.
anderson-heavenwards.webp: A young woman with golden hair looks upward, as if at something high above, among white flowers and pale sky. Anderson painted it in 1883. It is in a private collection.
anderson-at-the-well.webp: A young woman in white sits on the rocks by a spring, barefoot, with a clay water jar beside her. Anderson lived for more than twenty years on the island of Capri, and its country people often appear in her paintings. It is in a private collection.
anderson-the-flower-girl-capri.webp: A young woman with a basket of wild flowers stands on a rocky slope above the sea at Capri, where Anderson lived from 1871 until 1894. It is in a private collection.
anderson-simplicity.webp: A girl with flowing red-gold hair, a coral necklace and a fan sits in a red chair. Anderson painted it in her smooth, finely finished style. It is in a private collection.
landseer-favourites.webp: A grey horse, saddled and ready, waits in a stable yard with two dogs. They were the favourite animals of Prince George of Cambridge, Queen Victoria’s cousin. Landseer painted animals with such feeling that they seem to have characters of their own. The picture is in the Yale Center for British Art.
landseer-donald-mcintyre.webp: A Highlander in a kilt and a tartan bonnet sits at the mouth of a cave with his dogs. Landseer went back to Scotland again and again from 1824 on and loved its people and its hunting. The portrait is in the Yale Center for British Art.
landseer-a-highland-landscape.webp: A Scottish glen, with moorland, a winding river and mountains under storm clouds, painted quickly in oils on the spot. Landseer is known for his animals, but sketches like this show his love of the Highlands themselves. It is in the Yale Center for British Art.
landseer-deer-and-deer-hounds-in-a-mount: A stag and the hounds chasing it have plunged together into a mountain torrent and are swept down among the rocks. Landseer often painted the hunting of deer in the Highlands. The picture is in Tate Britain.
landseer-lion-defending-its-prey.webp: A lion stands over a dead deer and snarls at a great snake coiling towards it. Years later Landseer made the four bronze lions at the foot of Nelson’s Column in Trafalgar Square. This picture is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
A family at ease in a room with a view over a river: a man rests on a sofa, a woman reads beside a child, and a spaniel sleeps on the floor. Landseer was a favourite painter of English society, and their dogs seldom left his pictures out. It is in the National Gallery of Ireland in Dublin.
landseer-a-group-of-animals-geneva.webp: Under a stone arch, a white donkey, a mule in a tasselled headdress, horses and an ox with a woolly forelock crowd round a basket of greens, while a dog rests below. Landseer painted it in 1851, the year after he was knighted. It is in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
